a b s t r a c t

The aim of the current study was to examine associations between body appreciation and putative correlates that focus on self-enhancement and self-expression. Students (N = 261; mean age = 20.16 years, SD = 3.68; 60.9% female) from a non-residential college in the northeastern United States completed a questionnairemeasuring body appreciation,interestincosmetic enhancements, andneed foruniqueness. Individuals with higher body appreciation and African Americans/Blacks reported significantly higher self-attributed need for uniqueness and significantly higher investment in a distinctive appearance. The association between body appreciation and interest in cosmetic enhancements (e.g., hair coloring) was not significant. Results suggest that body appreciation may be linked to a desire to express one's own unique qualities.

Historically, body image research has focused on negative body image. Although important for understanding the pervasiveness of body concerns and potentially associated eating problems,this narrow focus failed to address the complexity of thoughts and feelings people may have about their bodies, including positive perceptions. Recent research has indicated that positive body image is in fact a separate construct from negative body image, with its own unique dimensions and correlates (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Tylka and Wood-Barcalow (2015a) define positive body image as body appreciation, loving and feeling comfort with one's body, having broad ideas of attractiveness, adaptive self-care for appearance, manifesting positive feelings through the body, and filtering information about the body in protective ways. Psychometrically sound measures have been developed to capture these constructs including body appreciation, the most widely studied aspect of positive body image (Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). The current study focused on associations between body appreciation and putative correlates that relate to the desire to enhance or to express one's appearance.
1.1. Body appreciation and interest in cosmetic enhancements

Body appreciation is associated with appearance-related attitudes and behaviors that are protective of health and well-being (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Individuals with higher body appreciation value, respect, and feel pride in their bodies more than those with lower body appreciation, suggesting that they may be better equipped to resist cultural pressure to meet unrealistic standards of attractiveness (Chrisler, Marvan, Gorman, & Rossini, 2015; Gillen, 2015). In resisting this pressure, they may be less accepting of, and engage less frequently in, behaviors that can help them meet a thin, toned, and tan ideal (Grant, Gillen, & Bernstein, 2014; Murnen, 2011). For example,those with higher body appreciation report significantly lower drive for muscularity and more sun protective attitudes (Gillen, 2015). Their behaviors are also more oriented toward health and well-being: they report significantly lower dieting behaviors,less disordered eating,higher intuitive eating (following their body's cues for hunger and satiety), less talk about dieting and weight loss, more sun protective behaviors, and more engagement in exercise (Andrew, Tiggemann, & Clark, 2016; Gillen, 2015; Tylka & Kroon Van Diest, 2013; Wasylkiw & Butler, 2014).

One appearance-related attitude that has not been frequently examinedis interestincosmetic enhancements.Cosmetic enhancements (e.g., manicures, genital waxing) are typically lower risk procedures, take relatively little time, and can be performed outside of a medical context by trained staff. Yet, perhaps contrary to common beliefs, these procedures, as well as some self-performed cosmetic enhancements (e.g., high-heeled shoes), can come with

health risks (Saltzberg & Chrisler, 1995). For example, some women have experienced toxic side effects from cosmetics (Saltzberg & Chrisler, 1995). Thus, cosmetic enhancements are pursued to improve appearance, yet come with some level of risk.

Given that body appreciation is associated with health protective attitudes and behaviors (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a), it is possible that individuals higher in body appreciation are less interested in cosmetic enhancements. Because individuals with higher body appreciation may conform less to culturally constructed appearance ideals (Gillen, 2015), they may be less interested in procedures aimed at achieving these ideals. Prior research provides support for this contention, although most of this work has focused on cosmetic surgery attitudes. These attitudes capture individuals' opinions on cosmetic surgery procedures, including their personal willingness to undergo these procedures. For example, body appreciation was significantly associated with lower acceptance of cosmetic surgery attitudes in university students from the United Kingdom and South Korea (Swami, 2009; Swami, Campana, & Coles, 2012; Swami, Hwang, & Jung, 2012), and in community samples of adults from Malaysia, Brazil, and the United States (U.S.) (Swami, 2010; Swami et al., 2011; Tylka & Iannantuono, 2016). However, body appreciation was not significantly associated with cosmetic surgery attitudes in adolescents in Sweden (Lunde, 2013), and in middle-aged women in the U.S. (Chrisler, Gorman, Serra, & Chapman, 2012).

Yet, little is known about associations between body appreciation and attitudes toward cosmetic enhancements. As previous literature on cosmetic surgery attitudes suggests (e.g., Swami, 2009), body appreciation may be associated with less interest in cosmetic enhancements, as cosmetic enhancements can help individuals conform to cultural ideals of attractiveness (albeit with lower risks than surgery). Another possibility is that cosmetic enhancements can help individuals express their unique qualities, and therefore interest in these procedures may be linked to higher body appreciation. For example, individuals may dye their hair blond or obtain genital waxing to conform to cultural ideals of beauty, or they might get a purple streak in their hair and their nails painted an unusual pattern to express uniqueness. Thus far, these associations have not been empirically tested.

We examined sex as a moderating factor in the association betweenbody appreciationandinterestincosmetic enhancements. That is, we explored the possibility that the associations between body appreciation and cosmetic enhancements might vary by sex. Women are significantly more interested in obtaining cosmetic procedures than men (Markey & Markey, 2010; Swami, Chamorro-Premuzic, Bridges, & Furnham, 2009; Swami et al., 2013). Yet body appreciation is linked to positive health outcomes for both men and women (Gillen, 2015), suggesting that it might be related to less interest in cosmetic enhancements for both sexes. Because these associations are not yet clear, in the current study, the modifying effect of sex on body appreciation and interest in cosmetic enhancements was explored.

In addition to body appreciation, it is important to consider the influence of several demographic variables on interest in cosmetic enhancements. In particular, body mass index (BMI) and race/ethnicity may be associated with interest in cosmetic enhancements. Because of the pervasive thin ideal in U.S. culture (Murnen, 2011), individuals who have higher BMIs may be more interested in cosmetic enhancements as methods for increasing perceived attractiveness. Cosmetic enhancements may allow individuals to feel attractive in ways that do not directly alter weight (e.g., hair dye). Although there is heterogeneity and variability within all racial/ethnic groups, previous research suggests that we might expect some between-group differences. African Americans are more satisfied with their appearance and bodies, and they are more cognitively and behaviorally invested in their appearance as

compared to European Americans, which may include spending time and effort on cosmetic enhancements (Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2012). Yet, previous research indicates that Caucasian women report greater acceptance of cosmetic surgery than their South Asian and African Caribbean female counterparts (Swami et al., 2012), suggesting that Caucasians may also be more interested in cosmetic enhancements than individuals in ethnicminority groups. Based on this previous work, we might expectthat European Americans/Whites or African Americans/Blacks may be more interested in cosmetic enhancements.
1.2. Body appreciation and need for uniqueness

Another variable related to self-enhancement/expression is need for uniqueness. We might expect that individuals with higher body appreciation would also be more interested in striving for and expressing their unique personal qualities. According to the theory of uniqueness (Snyder & Fromkin, 1977, p. 518), uniqueness is "a positive striving for differentness relative to other people", and should not be taken as a negative concept akin to abnormality and deviance, but rather one related to enhanced self-esteem. There are individual differences in the need for uniqueness; some individuals want to feel special and distinct more so than others do.

Tiggemann and Golder (2006) and Tiggemann and Hopkins (2011) applied the theory of uniqueness to tattooing, a form of body modification. Because tattooing is a means by which uniqueness can be displayed visibly on the body,they expected, and found, thatthose with atleast one tattoo had a significantly higher need for uniqueness than non-tattooed individuals. Swami (2012) reported similar findings. However, on distinctive appearance investment, a measure of the desire to have a noticeable, distinct appearance, Swami (2012) found that those who visited a tattoo parlor for their first tattoo had significantly higher distinctive appearance investment than those who visited a tattoo parlor and did not obtain a tattoo. Yet, Tiggemann and Golder (2006) found no significant differences on distinctive appearance investment between those with and without tattoos, and those with easily concealed, moderately visible, andno tattoos (Tiggemann &Hopkins,2011). Other research suggests that the process of acquiring a tattoo can increase feelings of uniqueness (Swami, 2011). Specifically, individuals reported significantly higher need for uniqueness and distinctive appearance investment several weeks after obtaining a tattoo (Swami, 2011).

As was done with tattooing, we can also extend the theory of uniqueness to body appreciation. The core features of body appreciation—acceptance, respect, and protection—provide a framework for understanding how one's body is unique in appearance and function (Tylka, 2011). Feeling as if one's body is special and distinct—whether for how it looks or what it can do—may be associated with a need for uniqueness. Some individuals have natural characteristics that are unusual (e.g., an uncommon name) that in turn predispose them to a higher need for distinctiveness (Lynn & Snyder, 2002). Individuals with higher body appreciation are unusual for having positive opinions about their body. Body image concerns are widespread among people of all ages including children and adults (Gillen & Markey, 2016). Within a cultural context of bodily discontent, body appreciation may setindividuals apart from others and therefore predispose them to a dispositional need for distinctiveness.

On the other hand, it is also possible that a higher need for uniqueness could lead individuals to appreciate their bodies more. For example, individuals who are higher in need for uniqueness are significantly more willing to take risks (Schumpe, Herzberg, & Erb, 2016); more extraverted, less neurotic, and open to new experiences (Schumpe et al., 2016; Swami, Hadji-Michael, & Furnham, 2008); more independent in their opinions (Snyder & Fromkin, 1977); have higher self-esteem (Gillen, 2015), and; strive

for uniqueness through consumption such as having a stronger desire for scarce, innovative, and customized products (Lynn & Harris, 1997). Such attitudes and behaviors reflecting a tendency toward assertiveness, socialness, and creativity could then promote higher body appreciation. Perhaps these individuals encounter more people and objects that are different from their own selves and experiences, and this leads them to appreciate body diversity, including how their own bodies fit within this framework. Or, their tendency to be social and noticeable in a positive way may invite more encouraging feedback from others that enhances their appreciation for their body.

A need for uniqueness among those with higher body appreciation may manifest more generally, as well as specifically in the domain of appearance. People are more interested in striving for uniqueness in areas that are salient to their self-concept (Lynn & Snyder, 2002). One of these domains is appearance. Appearance is likely an important domain for many people because the unrealistic images of men and women in popular culture suggest that there are beauty ideals to which all should aspire (Murnen, 2011). Although those with higher body appreciation may actively resist these ideals (Tylka, 2011), resistance nonetheless indicates cognitive effort in the appearance domain. Further, resistance of cultural ideals coupled with love and respect for the body, can develop into a defining aspect of the self because of its scarcity (Gillen & Markey, 2016). This reasoning suggests that those with higher body appreciation may have a high need for uniqueness in the specific realm of appearance. However, because links between body appreciation and need for uniqueness have not been explored previously, a general measure of need for uniqueness as well as one more specific to appearance (i.e., distinctive appearance investment; Tiggemann & Golder, 2006) were included in the current study.

We also examined the modifying effect of sex on body appreciation and need for uniqueness to determine if these associations are significant for both men and women or women only. Although no significant sex differences have been found on need for uniqueness and distinctive appearance investment (Swami, 2011), findings on body appreciation have been more variable, with some work showing significant (albeit small) sex differences and other work showing non-significant sex differences (Gillen, 2015; Swami et al., 2008; Tylka, 2013). Thus, previous empirical work does not inform hypotheses about how sex might act as a moderator in the relations between body appreciation and need for uniqueness, suggesting that this question is worth exploring in the current study.

In addition to body appreciation, we examined associations between several demographic variables and need for uniqueness. BMI may relate to need for uniqueness. Because individuals with larger BMIs do not meet cultural definitions of attractiveness (Murnen, 2011), they may have a stronger need to feel distinct so that they stand out in a positive way. This may be true on global measures of need for uniqueness, but it may be particularly evident on measures specific to appearance. Further, race/ethnicity may be relevant to need for uniqueness. African Americans/Blacks may have a stronger desire for uniqueness than those in other racial/ethnic groups. Parker et al. (1995) found that African American girls have more flexible ideas of beauty than White girls. In particular, African American girls' ideas of attractiveness include "looking good," or being well-kept, confident, and making your own assets work for you, suggesting that unique personal styles are desirable and something toward which to strive (Parker et al., 1995).
Drawing on research and theory on interest in cosmetic enhancements and need for uniqueness, we proposed two hypotheses. First, we hypothesized that individuals with higher

body appreciation would be less interested in cosmetic enhancements as compared to individuals with lower body appreciation. We explored interactions between body appreciation and sex. Second, we hypothesized that individuals with higher body appreciation would have a higher need for uniqueness, both general uniqueness and uniqueness specific to the appearance domain as compared to individuals with lower body appreciation. We explored interactions between body appreciation and sex.

Undergraduates enrolled at a regional college of a larger university in the northeastern United States participated in a study. Participants' mean age was M = 20.16 years (SD = 3.68), and 60.9% identified as women. The sample was racially/ethnically diverse with 44.4% identifying as European American/White (n = 116), 20.3% as Asian American/Asian/Pacific Islander (n = 53), 17.6% as African American/Black (n = 46), 8.0% as Latino/a American/Hispanic (n = 21), and 9.6% as other (n = 25). Prior to data collection, it was determined that a sample size of at least 250 was required in order to conduct the planned analyses. This determination was made based on recent literature suggesting that correlations tend to stabilize, in most situations, as sample sizes approach 250 (Schonbrodt ¨ & Perugini, 2013). The sample size for the current study was N = 261.

Participants reported their height and weight and from these data, BMI was calculated (see Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2016, for formula). Descriptive data on BMI from this sample were also measured and presented in Gillen (2015).

The Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos et al., 2005) was used to assess positive body image. The original 13-item measure was used because the second version ofthe measure (the Body Appreciation Scale-2; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015b) was not available at the time of data collection. This measure captures appreciation for the body (sample item: "I feel good about my body"), one aspect of the multifaceted construct of positive body image (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Although the BAS was initially created for use with women, scores on the scale were found to be invariant for U.S. men and women (Tylka, 2013), with differential item responding on one item. Responses were made on a 5-point scale (1 = Never to 5 = Always). Items were averaged to create a total score, with higher scores representing higher body appreciation. BAS scores have demonstrated satisfactory validity and reliability in previous studies of U.S. college students (Avalos et al., 2005; Tylka, 2013). Internal consistency reliability scores in the current study were adequate (Cronbach's ˛: women ˛= .92, men ˛= .90). Descriptive data on body appreciation from this sample were also measured and presented in Gillen (2015).

A subscale from the Interest in Cosmetic Surgery Scale (Markey & Markey, 2009) was used to assess interest in cosmetic enhancements. This subscale contains 6 items and measures interest in obtaining cosmetic procedures that are typically low in cost and invasiveness, do not require a large time commitment, and do not need to be performed in a medical context. The items were: facial, manicure, pedicure,facial waxing (hair removal on face using wax, e.g., eyebrows), genital waxing (hair removal on genital area

The Distinctive Appearance Investment Scale (Tiggemann & Golder, 2006) was used to measure desire for uniqueness in the appearance domain (sample items: "I use my physical appearance to express who I am," "When it comes to appearance, I am somewhat of a non-conformist."). It has 6 items to which participants respond ona 5-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree). Items were averaged to create a total score, with higher scores indicating stronger desire for a unique appearance. Previous research demonstrates the validity and reliability of scores on this measure in men and women (Swami, 2011; Tiggemann & Golder, 2006; Tiggemann & Hopkins, 2011). Internal consistency reliability scores in the current study were adequate (women ˛= .76, men ˛= .82).

The Self-Attributed Need for Uniqueness Scale (Lynn & Harris, 1997) was used to measure desire for uniqueness. Unlike the Distinctive Appearance Investment Scale (Tiggemann & Golder, 2006), it is a more general measure of desire for uniqueness not limited to the appearance domain. Although it was developed for consumer research (Lynn & Harris, 1997), it has been used previously in body image research (Swami, 2011). It has 4 "fill-in the-blank" items to which participants respond on a 5-point scale. Response options differ across items (sample item: "Being distinctive is important to me." a = Not at all, b = Slightly, c = Moderately, d = Very, e = Extremely). Items were averaged to create a total score, with higher scores indicating stronger desire for uniqueness. Scores on this measure have shown satisfactory validity and reliability in men and women in previous studies (Lynn & Harris, 1997; Swami, 2011). Internal consistency reliability scores in the current study were adequate (women ˛= .75, men ˛= .73).

After giving informed consent, participants completed a paperand-pencil questionnaire on campus in a group setting, supervised by members of the research team. Participants' responses were not linked to their names. Students were recruited from a participant pool at the college, so they elected to participate for course credit in one of several foundational courses in psychology. The study was advertised as a research study about body modification in college students with the purpose being to learn about college

students' attitudes and behaviors related to body modification. Measures were presented in the same order for all participants. Other measures in the study pertain to body image, body modification (e.g., piercings and tattoos), risk behaviors and attitudes, and mental health. The Institutional Review Board (IRB) at the university approved this study.

All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS v.24 for Windows. All p-values <.05 were considered statistically significant, and twotailed p-values are reported for all hypothesis tests. We initially assessed the data for missing values. Participants with more than 20%oftheir datamissing were excluded fromall analyses. Using Little's test(Little, 1988),the remainingmissing data were determined to be missing completely at random (MCAR). We used pooled estimates from multiple imputation, using all relevant study variables in the imputation model and 20 iterations, to replace the remaining missing data. Following replacement ofthe missing values, data were assessed for entry errors and significant outliers (±3 SD). No entry errors or significant outliers were found and therefore no further changes were made to the data.

Independent samples t-tests were conducted to assess differences in key study variables for men and women, and one-way analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were used to determine racial/ethnic differences in these same variables. All ANOVA models met the appropriate assumptions (e.g., normality, homogeneity of variance). To control for Type I error, Tukey HSD post hoc pairwise comparisons were used. Partial eta-squared (-p2) was used to estimate effect sizes of the ANOVAs, using guidelines suggested by Ferguson (2009; small = .04; medium = .25;large = .64). Cohen's d was used to estimate effect sizes ofthe pairwise comparisons, using guidelines suggested by Cohen (1988; small = 0.20; medium = 0.50; large = 0.80). Bivariate correlations were used to examine the associations among key study variables. Stepwise linear regression models were used to test the hypotheses. To avoid issues with multicollinearity, all variables used in the regression models were mean-centered. All regression models met the appropriate regression assumptions (e.g., normality, VIF levels).

Table 1 shows mean scores for all analytic variables separated by sex. A series of Bonferroni-corrected t-tests were used to test for significant sex differences. Men had significantly higher body appreciation than women (d = 0.47; medium effect), and women were significantly more interested in cosmetic enhancements than men (d = 2.96; large effect). Men and women did not differ significantly on BMI, need for uniqueness, and distinctive appearance investment.

Five one-way ANOVAs were conducted to test for mean differences in key study variables across racial/ethnic groups (see Table 2). There were no significant racial/ethnic differences in body appreciation or in BMI (ps > .05). However, overall models revealed small significant differences between the groups in need for uniqueness, F(4, 256) = 6.92, p < .001, p2 = .10, distinctive appearance investment, F(4, 256) = 4.96, p = .001, p2 = .07, and interest in cosmetic enhancements, F(4, 256) = 2.98, p = .020, p2 = .05. Post hoc Tukey HSD pair-wise comparisons revealed that African American/Black participants reported significantly higher need for uniqueness and distinctive appearance investment (all ps < .047, ds = 0.71–.84; large effects) when compared to all other racial/ethnic groups with the exception of those identifying as 'other.' For interest in cosmetic enhancements, the only significant difference was betweenAsianAmerican/Asian/Pacific Islanders and Latino/a Americans/Hispanics (p = .038, d = 0.81; large effect), in that Latino/a Americans/Hispanics reported greater interest in cosmetic enhancements than Asian American/Asian/Pacific Islanders. Because of these significant group differences, race/ethnicity is examined as predictor in all subsequent regression analyses.

Next, correlations were performed to illustrate bivariate associations between variables, and were conducted separately by sex (see Table 1). In men, higher body appreciation was significantly associated with both lower BMI and higher self-attributed need for uniqueness, although the associations were weak. In women, higher body appreciation was significantly associated with lower BMI, higher self-attributed need for uniqueness, and higher distinctive appearance investment, although the associations were again weak.

Next,two linear regressions were performed to illustrate associations between key study variables and to determine the amount of variance accounted for in the outcomes by body appreciation (see Table 3). In order to use race/ethnicity as a predictor variable in the regression models, we created five dummy variables. In the analyses, European American/White was omitted and thus served as the reference category for each racial/ethnic group. Demographic variables including sex, BMI, and the five dummy coded race/ethnicity variables were entered in Step 1, body appreciation was entered in Step 2, and body appreciation × sex was entered in Step 3. The outcomes were self-attributed need for uniqueness and distinctive appearance investment (because body appreciation was not significantly associated with interest in cosmetic enhancements, we omitted the regression model with interest in cosmetic enhancements as the outcome). Step 2 (but not Step 3) added a significant amount of variance in both regression models (see Table 3). Individuals with higher body appreciation and those who identified as African American/Black reported significantly higher distinctive appearance investment and significantly higher self-attributed need for uniqueness.
The goal of the current study was to explore associations between body appreciation and variables that reflect self-

enhancement and/or self-expression,including interestincosmetic enhancements and need for uniqueness. Results generally suggested that individuals with higher body appreciation also tended to show a stronger need for uniqueness. Body appreciation was associated with a greater desire for uniqueness both generally and in the domain of appearance; these findings emerged once the effects of sex, BMI, and race/ethnicity had been accounted for. Body appreciation was not significantly associated with interest in cosmetic enhancements.

Body appreciation significantly predicted both uniqueness variables: distinctive appearance investment and self-attributed need for uniqueness. Distinctive appearance investment includes the need to stand out in the domain of appearance. People strive to be unique in domains that are more integral to their sense of self (Lynn & Snyder, 2002). Appearance may be particularly important to those with higher body appreciation, but not just for aesthetic reasons. Individuals with higher body appreciation may value their bodies for what they can do, as well as the special combination of features they have that comprise their unique selves. Feeling a close connection with and sense of appreciation for one's body (Tylka, 2011) may be related to wanting to publically express its perceived special qualities.

Self-attributed need for uniqueness is a more general measure of need for uniqueness, and also demonstrated significant associations with body appreciation. That is, individuals with higher body appreciation also tended to show a higher need to be distinct. The Self-Attributed Need for Uniqueness Scale is a relatively brief measure that does not specify domains in which individuals strive for uniqueness. Yet, it appears that individuals' need for uniqueness extends beyond the domain of appearance into a more general need to feel different from others. Being different might lead to being challenged by others for one's unique characteristics, and therefore requires a degree of confidence in upholding these same qualities. As supported by the theory of uniqueness (Snyder & Fromkin, 1977), striving for difference is a positive process related to higher self-esteem. Previous research also demonstrates that body appreciation is significantly associated with characteristics that are conducive to self-expression such as higher self-esteem (Gillen, 2015), lower neuroticism (Swami et al., 2008), higher extraversion (Swami et al., 2008), lower maladaptive perfectionism (Iannantuono & Tylka, 2012), greater sexual liberalism and more positive attitudes toward unconventional sexual practices (Swami, Weis, Barron, & Furnham, 2017). Thus, body appreciation may encourage confidence that allows people to strive for difference. It is also possible that the mere presence of body appreciation is a unique quality. It is normative for people to have body image concerns (Gillen &Markey, 2016), and less common to score high on measures of positive body image, at least among women (Wood-Barcalow, Tylka, & Augustus-Horvath, 2010). Amidst widespread body concerns, higher body appreciation may set individuals apart from others. Naturally unusual qualities (i.e., body appreciation) may, over time, instill in people a trait level need for distinctiveness (Lynn & Snyder, 2002). It is important to consider,

however, that the need for uniqueness may be culturally-bound. Individuals in cultures with independent construals of the self, like the U.S., may be more prone to strive for uniqueness than those in cultures that encourage interdependent perspectives of the self (Markus & Kitayama, 1991). Future research should focus on associations between body appreciation and need for uniqueness in non-Western cultures that are more oriented toward interdependent selves.

Interestingly, body appreciation was not associated with interest in cosmetic enhancements. Cosmetic enhancements (e.g., genital waxing,hair coloring) arenot very time consuming or costly, and are generally easily accessible and low in risk. Therefore, body appreciation may not distinguish those who are interested in pursuing these relatively commonplace procedures from those who are not. Another potential explanation for the lack of association between body appreciation and interestin cosmetic enhancements is the meaning individuals attach to these procedures. Some may engage in them to achieve cultural ideals of beauty, some may obtain them to achieve a distinct appearance, whereas others may see them as a form of self-care. These different motives may wash out any significant associations between these variables.

Results from the regressions also showed that African Americans/Blacks had significantly higher need for uniqueness, both generally and in the domain of appearance. This finding is consistent with previous research illustrating that African American girls value and strive for utilizing and expressing the unique aspects of one's appearance (Parker et al., 1995). Striving for uniqueness is a positive process related to improved self-esteem (Snyder &

Fromkin, 1977), and may explain why African Americans/Blacks tend to have more positive body image than those in other racial/ethnic groups, particularly European Americans/Whites (Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2012; Parker et al., 1995; Swami,Airs, Chouhan, Leon, & Towell, 2009). This finding may also reflect Majors and Billson's (1992) work on African American men, who adapt a 'cool pose' in an effort to distinguish their identities in a culture that limits their opportunities for success. Thus, for some oppressed groups, appearance is a controllable domain through which they can express their unique qualities (Gillen & Lefkowitz, 2006).

The present study has limitations. It is correlational and therefore does not allow conclusions to be drawn regarding the direction of associations. For example, body appreciation may lead individuals to strive for uniqueness, just as need for uniqueness may also be conducive to appreciating one's body. These associations may also be confounded by third variables such as personality and selfesteem. The measure of cosmetic enhancements is limited in scope (i.e., 6 items) and could be expanded to include other procedures, including some that may be more common in men, and some that could better reflect need for uniqueness (e.g., adding items on type/color of hair dye). In addition, our results are not widely generalizable. Although not available at the time of data collection, there is a newer version of the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS-2; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015b) that addresses some of the limitations of the original BAS and incorporates new information gleaned from the positive body image literature. This newer measure may have better captured body appreciation in our sample.

A strength of the current study is its focus on several putative correlates of body appreciation that focus on self-enhancement and/or expression that have not been frequently examined in prior research. Results show that individuals with higher body appreciation also had a stronger desire to be different from others which may represent an underlying confidence in themselves and their bodies. Future studies should continue to focus on associations between body appreciation and need for uniqueness. It would be interesting, for example, to examine if body appreciation is associated with markers that signify a unique appearance such as tattoos, piercings, facial cosmetics, and clothing styles (Tiggemann & Golder, 2006; Tiggemann & Hopkins, 2011). Potential mediators of the links between body appreciation and need for uniqueness could also be explored including self-esteem and personality traits (e.g., extraversion). The present findings add to the growing literature on positive body image by indicating that body appreciation is related to indicators of "positive striving for differentness" (Snyder & Fromkin, 1977, p. 518)
